lead: Every die leaving the fab is good or bad, and nothing outside says which. Test applies inputs, reads outputs and compares them with what a good chip should give, so bad chips are removed before a customer pays. Test costs a machine, a program and seconds per chip. This chapter covers defects and failures, the test floor, and the yield-and-coverage arithmetic that sets how many bad chips escape.
prereq: You need: only the picture of a fabricated wafer full of die from Unit 2, CMOS Fabrication and Layout.

sections.h3: From a physical defect to a customer failure

blocks.text: A wafer holds hundreds or thousands of die: some perfect, some dead, most in between. Test drives known values on the input pins, samples outputs on a stated clock, and compares each result with the value in the test program. A mismatch means the chip misses its specification.
Four words describe the chain from a speck of dust to a returned product.

head: Term
What it is
Example
rows: A physical flaw in the manufactured structure
A dust particle breaks one metal wire, leaving it open
The logical behaviour of that defect
The broken wire acts like a node stuck at 0 (see 6.2)
A wrong value at a node at a particular time
The adder drives 0110 where 0111 is expected
Loss of the function the customer bought

blocks.text: One defect creates faults; a fault produces errors when the circuit is exercised; an error reaching an output pin becomes a failure the tester sees. Good test makes that happen in the factory, not in the field.

Verification simulates the design (Unit 5) and asks whether the logic is correct. Test measures a physical chip and asks whether this copy was built right. A design can pass every simulation and still fail on the tester, because the fab produced what the netlist never described: a short, an open, a missing contact. Verification catches design bugs; test catches manufacturing defects.
ATE, automatic test equipment, is the machine: pin electronics that drive and sense every chip pin, a precise timing generator, programmable power supplies, and a computer running the test program.

items: DUT: the device under test, the chip being measured now.
Probe card: fine needles that land on bond pads, so die are tested before packaging.
Device interface board (DIB): plugs into the tester and routes its channels to the socket or probe card.
Handler: lifts packaged chips from a tray, presses each into a socket at set temperature, and drops it into a pass or fail bin.

blocks.text: A tester has more channels than one chip needs, so one program drives many die at once. In multi-site testing with s sites in parallel, the time charged per die falls by a factor of s.
test cost per die = (R × t) / s
blocks.where: R is the running cost of the tester in rupees per second (depreciation, power, floor space, operator); t is the test time for one die in seconds; s is the number of sites tested in parallel.

blocks.text: Four costs add up: the tester, charged per second; test time per die, from milliseconds for a small analog part to seconds for a large SoC; engineering cost of vectors, paid once per design; and overkill, the loss when a good die fails a marginal measurement.

sections.h3: Yield, fault coverage and defect level

blocks.text: Yield Y is the fraction of die on a wafer that meet specification. It falls as die area grows, because a random defect anywhere on a larger die kills it (Unit 2).

Fault coverage T is the fraction of listed faults that the vector set detects. The list comes from a fault model (6.2); T is measured by fault simulation (6.3). Some syllabi call it test coverage. No real program reaches T = 1.

blocks.where: DL is the defect level, the fraction of shipped parts that are actually bad; Y is the yield, a fraction between 0 and 1; T is the fault coverage, also between 0 and 1; the exponent is (1 − T).
DPM is defective parts per million shipped; DL is the defect level as a fraction.

blocks.text: The formula treats surviving defects as independent and assumes the test detects a random fraction T of them, letting a fraction (1 − T) escape. Clustering makes the result an estimate, not a guarantee, but the shape is right: as T rises towards 1, the exponent (1 − T) shrinks and DL falls steeply.

sections.h3: Quality, reliability and the four test stages

blocks.text: Quality describes parts at shipping: how many are bad, in DPM. Reliability describes parts after shipping: how long they keep working, in FIT, failures per 10⁹ device-hours.

The failure rate follows the bathtub curve. Infant mortality is a high, falling failure rate in the first weeks, from weak oxide, bad vias and contamination. Useful life is a long, low, almost flat rate. Wear-out is a rising rate at end of life, from electromigration and oxide breakdown. Burn-in runs chips for hours at high temperature and raised voltage so infant mortality happens in the factory; retest then removes the dead.

items: Silicon debug: first silicon on a bench, hunting design bugs.
Characterisation: delay, power and margins across voltage and temperature corners, for the datasheet.
Production test: every chip, every lot, on the ATE.
Incoming inspection: the customer's sampling check on a received lot.

examples.question: A wafer lot has yield Y = 0.90. The production test program has fault coverage T = 0.95. (a) Find the defect level in DPM. (b) Repeat for a program with T = 0.99. (c) By what factor does the number of shipped defective parts fall?
steps: Formula: DL = 1 − Y^(1−T), with Y = 0.90 and 1 − T = 0.05.
examples.answer: About 5254 DPM at T = 0.95 and about 1053 DPM at T = 0.99, a fall by a factor of about 5.
examples.check:
import math
Y = 0.90
for T in (0.95, 0.99):
    DL = 1 - Y ** (1 - T)
    print(round(DL * 1e6, 2))
print(round((1 - Y ** 0.05) / (1 - Y ** 0.01), 2))

traps: Assuming 100 % fault coverage means zero escaped chips. No real vector set reaches T = 1, and T counts only the faults the model listed.
Swapping yield and fault coverage. Yield is a fab property (good die out of total); fault coverage is a test-program property (faults detected out of faults listed).
Confusing the chain: defect is physical, fault is logical, error is a wrong node value, failure is lost function at the output.
A unit slip in DPM. DL = 0.005 is 5000 DPM: multiply by 10⁶, not 10⁴.
A clean simulation run does not prove the silicon works. Simulation verifies the netlist; only the tester sees the manufactured chip.

quiz.q: Define defect, fault, error and failure, one line each, with one example of each.
quiz.a: Defect: a physical flaw, such as a broken wire. Fault: its logical behaviour, such as a node stuck at 0. Error: a wrong value at a node at a given time, such as 0110 instead of 0111. Failure: loss of the function the customer needs, such as a blank display.

quiz.q: Expand ATE, DUT and DIB, and state what a handler does.
quiz.a: Automatic test equipment, device under test, device interface board. The handler takes packaged chips from a tray, holds each in a socket at a controlled temperature, and sorts it into a pass bin or a fail bin.

quiz.q: A design passes a million simulated vectors. Explain why its first silicon may still fail on the tester.
quiz.a: Simulation checks the netlist, not the manufactured structure. The fab can create shorts, opens, missing contacts and parameter shifts the netlist never contained. Verification proves the logic; test proves this copy was built correctly.

quiz.q: Why is burn-in run at final test rather than at wafer probe?
quiz.a: Burn-in means hours of powered, heated running. Packaged parts load into burn-in boards in thousands, and the parts stressed are exactly the ones that would ship. Retest after burn-in removes the ones that died, so infant mortality happens in the factory.

quiz.q: Distinguish quality from reliability, and name the unit used for each.
quiz.a: Quality is how many parts are good at the moment of shipping, measured in DPM (defective parts per million). Reliability is how long the parts keep working after shipping, measured in FIT (failures per 10⁹ device-hours).

quiz.q: A lot has yield Y = 0.95 and the test program has fault coverage T = 0.90. Find the defect level and the DPM.
A team has budget for one improvement only: raise yield from 0.80 to 0.90, or raise coverage from 0.90 to 0.99. Use DL = 1 − Y^(1−T) to say which ships fewer bad parts, and explain why.
quiz.a: Start at Y = 0.80, T = 0.90: 1 − 0.80^0.10 = 0.02207, about 22 070 DPM. Raise yield only (Y = 0.90, T = 0.90): 1 − 0.90^0.10 = 0.01048, about 10 480 DPM, a 2.1× fall. Raise coverage only (Y = 0.80, T = 0.99): 1 − 0.80^0.01 = 0.00223, about 2230 DPM, a 9.9× fall. Coverage wins because (1 − T) is the small exponent, and shrinking it multiplies the effect, while yield enters as the base and moves more slowly.

beyond: Not for the exam. Test engineering is its own career, and on large digital chips test is one of the biggest line items after silicon area. The defect-level formula is usually called the Williams–Brown model, and it lets a team argue how many vectors are worth paying for. Commercial EDA tools do fault simulation and automatic pattern generation, and IEEE 1500 wraps embedded cores so they can be tested from outside. Research pushes adaptive test: using earlier wafer or lot results to decide how long to test the next one. Search 'Williams-Brown defect level', 'test cost model VLSI' and 'adaptive test semiconductor'.
